_how_to_use: Add places you (Stached), a trusted client (Scouted), or a direct check (Vetted) can vouch for. The name must match what appears in itineraries. Stached: set stached:true for anywhere you've personally been and vouch for — a blog post isn't required. If you HAVE written it up, also add blog_link, the direct URL to that specific post on wanderingmustache.com, never the bare homepage or a category page; travelers see it as an 'Our write-up' link, so it must open the actual write-up. Leave blog_link blank ('') if there's no post — the place still gets the Stached badge, just without a link. Scouted needs client_feedback (positive only). Vetted needs verification_method plus verified_date (phone/email) or rating of 4.5+. our_take is the Wandering Mustache one-liner from the post's Links section; travelers see it next to the stamp, good or bad.

places.name: JW Marriott El Convento Cusco
places.our_take: The Stache pick, for a reason. Built on the site of the ancient colonial convent of San Agustín, it’s a living museum. Ask for a room with an original Inca wall; there is nothing quite like waking up next to 500-year-old stonework that’s still more structurally sound than most modern skyscrapers.

places.name: Belmond Hotel Monasterio
places.our_take: A literal 16th-century monastery where the courtyard is so peaceful you’ll forget you’re gasping for air.

places.name: Belmond Palacio Nazarenas
places.our_take: The city’s only outdoor heated pool, plus oxygen-enriched rooms — a godsend for those who enjoy breathing.

places.name: Plaza de Armas
places.our_take: The beating heart of Cusco, and a constant theater of parades, festivals and people in colorful traditional dress. Sit, watch, and do not attempt the stairs on the way back to the hotel too quickly.

places.name: Qorikancha (Temple of the Sun)
places.our_take: The most sacred of all Inca sites, and the church here still displays many original Inca ruins. What you walk through is only a portion of what stood here before the Spanish invasion; the floors and walls were said to be covered in gold and silver. The ultimate “before and after” of Peruvian history. Avenida El Sol s/n · +51 84 249176

places.name: Twelve Angled Stone
places.our_take: A stone in the middle of town with twelve angle cuts, each one fitted to its neighbors. The Inca had no metal tools for cutting stone. Their precision is hard to replicate even with today’s tools, and it’s free to stare at.

places.name: Inka Museum
places.our_take: An excellent overview of the Inca empire. Go here first and the rest of the city makes more sense.

places.name: Museo Casa Concha
places.our_take: A great museum with artifacts from Machu Picchu. If you’ve just been to the citadel, this is where the pieces ended up.

places.name: Traditional Textile Center of Cusco
places.our_take: If you can’t get to one of the weaving cooperatives in the Sacred Valley, this is an excellent place to learn the tradition, watch a demonstration and buy from local artisans. Most items carry the weaver’s name.

places.name: Sacsayhuamán Archaeological Park
places.our_take: Perched on the hill overlooking the city. Technically a fortress, famous for massive stones that fit together so perfectly you couldn’t slide a credit card between them. You can walk to it: a 15-minute uphill walk from the Plaza, or a very short taxi ride. Calle Don Bosco s/n · +51 84 223077

places.name: JW Marriott Lima
places.our_take: The newly renovated standout for any five-star-preferred Marriott loyalist in Lima. We had an unplanned night here post-renovation during the 2025 trip and immediately understood why. The central location in Miraflores is the difference-maker: steps from the best restaurants in Barranco and Miraflores, walkable to the Malecón, positioned perfectly to explore without constant Uber rides. The renovation brought the property fully into the modern luxury space while keeping the service standards Marriott loyalists expect. If you’re Titanium or above, this is now the automatic choice. Av. José Larco 160, Miraflores · +51 1 217 7000

places.name: The Westin Lima
places.our_take: We’ve stayed here twice — 2022 and 2025 — and our opinion has shifted. The hotel itself is solid: newer, well run, excellent staff, good bar and restaurant. But the location is its real drawback for leisure travelers. San Isidro’s financial-district vibe doesn’t offer the walkability or neighborhood character you’re looking for in Lima, and the Uber to Miraflores and Barranco is 45 minutes to an hour at any normal hour of the day. We didn’t fully grasp this in 2022, but by 2025 the traffic reality was impossible to ignore. If you’re in town for business and San Isidro restaurants are your priority, this works. If you’re coming for the food and the neighborhoods, the location tax is real. Av. Coronel La Rosa 350, San Isidro · +51 1 201 5000

places.name: Miraflores Park, Belmond
places.our_take: A lovely, old-school hotel at the edge of Miraflores, next to Barranco. Very close to everything, but a world away from it all. Maintains the polished Belmond look and excellent service. If you want the security and prestige of a luxury brand with coastal positioning, this is it.

places.name: AC Hotel Miraflores
places.our_take: A good option if you want a familiar brand at a slightly lower price. Excellent location in Miraflores without the luxury-hotel price tag.

places.name: Wyndham Grand Costa del Sol Lima Airport
places.our_take: Because of flight timing, you may want to stay near the airport to avoid the hour-plus morning drive. This is our recommendation for airport stays. Note: there are two Wyndhams. You want the Grand.

places.name: San Francisco Convent & Catacombs
places.our_take: A haunting experience: bone-filled catacombs beneath this 17th-century convent in Centro Histórico. The underground passages hold thousands of skeletal remains arranged in haunting patterns. It’s both museum and memento mori. Plan one to two hours and book ahead in peak season. Jirón Lampa, Cercado de Lima · +51 1 427 1703

places.name: Larco Museum
places.our_take: A wonderfully curated small museum in Pueblo Libre with an excellent range of pre-Columbian exhibits — ceramics, textiles, and artifacts that illuminate Peru’s ancient civilizations, without the overwhelming scale of the larger museums. Set in a restored colonial mansion, with a lovely café. Worth half a day. (The khipu below, an Inca recording system of knotted strings used to track census data, tribute, and history, is one of the highlights.) Av. Simón Bolívar 1515, Pueblo Libre · +51 1 461 1312

places.name: Magic Water Circuit
places.our_take: A unique park in central Lima with incredible fountains that light up after dark. The evening laser show is genuinely impressive. Touristy, yes, but the engineering and artistry are worth experiencing. Go at dusk to catch both day and night. Parque de la Reserva, Lima · +51 1 330 3052

places.name: Huaca Pucllana
places.our_take: A 1,500-year-old pyramid in the middle of Miraflores, still imposing despite the modern development around it. Walk the site during the day to understand the scale, then return at night when it’s lit. The on-site restaurant has views of the illuminated pyramid. Calle General Borgoño cuadra 8, Miraflores · +51 1 617 7148

places.name: Maido
places.our_take: One of the best restaurants in Lima, with prices to prove it, and still He-Stache’s favorite. Chef Mitsuharu “Micha” Tsumura has perfected Nikkei cuisine (Japanese-Peruvian fusion) in a way few restaurants ever have. High-end, creative, and worth every penny if you can get a table. The flaw: they no longer offer gluten-free options. Calle San Martín 399, Miraflores · +51 1 313 5100

places.name: Central
places.our_take: Dining at a whole other level: a carefully crafted lesson in Peru’s megadiversity from chefs Virgilio Martínez and Pía León, one of the world’s most creative and innovative teams. The meal is presented as pure education — several courses show you the ingredient in its original form before it’s transformed into the dish. The flaw: the price has more than doubled in the past two years. At over $400 per person, food only, it’s out of reach for most visitors, let alone locals. We’re very glad we did it before the jump. Av. Pedro de Osma 301, Barranco · +51 1 242 8515

places.name: Kjolle
places.our_take: A standout within the Central group. We thoroughly enjoyed our meal here and feel it’s a much better deal than Central. If you can only do one, this is the spot — though we believe the price has doubled recently here, too. Chef Pía León showcases colorful and rare native flora in an ingredient-driven, innovative approach to Peruvian cuisine. Av. Pedro de Osma 301, Barranco · +51 1 242 8575

places.name: Mayta
places.our_take: A beautiful restaurant with many elevated Peruvian dishes and a very good cocktail menu: refined contemporary Peruvian cooking that transforms traditional recipes using local products. Av. Mariscal La Mar 1285, Miraflores · +51 937 220 734

places.name: Astrid y Gastón
places.our_take: We have not eaten here, but we had to include it: it’s truly an OG of Lima’s culinary revolution, and the restaurant that helped launch the city’s global reputation with refined Peruvian classics. Av. Paz Soldán 290, San Isidro · +51 1 442 2777

We expected to watch the Mexican folkloric dance, but the only seats were on stairs, which proved difficult for Dad. We opted for the mariachi band and dining on the sand instead. By far the best meal we had when you weigh cost against quality, and the mariachi band and service were both very good.

places.name: Joya (Cirque du Soleil)
places.destination: Riviera Maya, Cancun, Playa del Carmen, Tulum, Mexico
places.our_take: Cirque du Soleil’s first Latin American show, now with a dinner option. We were pleasantly surprised by the quality and creativity of the food. Unfortunately, the three-course dinner was crammed into a 45-minute pre-show sprint. It just doesn’t work, and it took away from both the meal and the entertainment.

places.name: Le Petit Chef
